newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania meets IMF criteria for new loans-PM.
newsitem.headline: Romania meets IMF criteria for new loans-PM.

text.p: Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea on Wednesday said Romania was meeting all targets set down by international lenders and was on course for eventual European Union membership.
But Ciorbea complained that the EU was unfairly proceeding with its eastward expansion in "waves" and vowed to foster reforms to reverse a decision to deny Romania early entry.
"All conditions agreed with the International Monetary Fund in a memorandum have been met," Ciorbea told a news conference. "There is no risk whatsoever in delaying further IMF tranches."

Ciorbea made his remarks as an International Monetary Fund technical team arrived for a three-week mission to monitor the progress of reforms undertaken earlier this year after the election of a centrist parliament and president.
A first tranche of $86 million, under a 13-month stand-by agreement worth a total $430 million, was released in April.
The Fund's chief negotiator for Romania, Poul Thomsen, arrives next week to determine whether Romania has met conditions for releasing the second of five such disbursements.
A second IMF review is due early in 1998.

Ciorbea said Romania would press on with reforms to persuade the EU to reconsider plans, announced in Strasbourg, to limit initial membership talks to five ex-communist states -- Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Estonia and Slovenia -- and Cyprus.
"We will continue our political and diplomatic fight right through until December," he said in reference to the final EU enlargement decision to be taken at a summit in Luxembourg.

Romania had concentrated its efforts on early entry to NATO, assuming its criteria were easier to fulfil. Last week's NATO summit in Madrid also left Romania out, inviting only Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.

Ciorbea said his government had met many of the objectives stipulated by the IMF, including a stable currency, a fall in the inflation rate to 2.3 percent in June from more than 30 percent in March and controlling the budget deficit.
"One can see elements of macroeconomic stability here," he said during a three-hour exchange with reporters.

Also to the government's credit, he said, were legislation to boost foreign investment and capital inflows which helped revive the bourse and pushed the central bank's foreign exchange reserves above $2 billion.

Romania's centrist government, elected last November after seven years of rule by leftists, has pledged to cut the current account deficit to $1.4 billion from last year's $2.3 billion, increase foreign exchange reserves, speed up privatisation and privatise at least one bank.
The Fund suspended credits last year, saying the leftist government of the time had overspent and hobbled foreign exchange markets ahead of the election it eventually lost.
The World Bank, which also withheld loans last year, has approved $550 million in credits to help restructure farming, upgrade infrastructure and cushion the effects of reforms.

Ciorbea said the government's efforts had so far produced few tangible results, with inventories piling up and low industrial performance, but added: "You have to admit that nobody can do in seven months what others required years to accomplish."
Recent polls suggest that Romanians are willing to proceed with reforms despite average monthly salaries equivalent to less than $80.
